results.claim: Max-Bounded-Sums is linearly equivalent to selecting the largest offset whose contiguous equal-offset prefix-array mixed differences all meet the threshold.
results.proof_sketch: Index A from 1 and define P_ij=sum_{r<=i,c<=j} A_rc, with P_0j=P_i0=0. For 1<=l<=q and 0<=i<=m-l, 0<=j<=n-l, define D_l(i,j)=P_{i+l,j+l}-P_{i+l,j}-P_{i,j+l}+P_{i,j}. Inclusion-exclusion gives D_l(i,j)=sum_{r=i+1}^{i+l} sum_{c=j+1}^{j+l} A_rc. Thus F_l=max_{i,j} D_l(i,j), and the requested answer is exactly max({l: every D_l(i,j)<=k} union {0}). The map A to P takes O(mn) arithmetic/word operations. Conversely, every integer P with zero top and left boundaries yields A_ij=P_ij-P_{i-1,j}-P_{i,j-1}+P_{i-1,j-1}; telescoping recovers P in O(mn). Hence algorithms for either formulation transfer to the other with only linear work. This is a k-relaxed Monge-defect test restricted to contiguous square offsets.

results.claim: An alleged optimum has a linear-time verifiable certificate, even for arbitrary signed entries.
results.proof_sketch: Let q=min(m,n), and let F_l be the maximum sum of an l by l square. Adopt L=0 when no positive length is feasible. Build the two-dimensional prefix-sum table in O(mn) time. A certificate for optimum L consists of: (i) for every l>L, coordinates of one l-square having sum greater than k; and (ii) no additional data for L. Verification checks all (m-L+1)(n-L+1) L-squares have sum at most k (vacuous for L=0), and checks the supplied witness for each l>L. Every sum is obtained from four prefix entries. Thus verification costs O(mn+q)=O(mn) arithmetic/word operations. The first condition proves L feasible, while the witnesses prove every larger length infeasible, so the characterization is exact.

results.claim: There is an exact output-sensitive search algorithm whose worst-case time is O(mn min(m,n)).
results.proof_sketch: After prefix-sum preprocessing, inspect lengths q,q-1,...,1. For each l, scan its square placements until finding a sum greater than k; retain that placement as the infeasibility witness. Return the first l for which the entire scan finds no violation, or 0 if every length has a witness. Correctness follows directly from descending order. If m>=n=q, the optimum is L, and d=q-L, the number of tested placements is at most sum_{t=0}^d (m-n+t+1)(t+1), hence the total time is O(mn+(m-n+1)(d+1)^2+(d+1)^3). This is O(mnq) in the worst case and O(mn) whenever d=O(1). When L=0, the displayed sum includes one harmless extra t=q term. The algorithm also constructs the certificate in the preceding claim.

results.claim: Positive-length feasibility has no universal cross-length structure: every Boolean pattern is realizable with O(log q)-bit signed entries.
results.proof_sketch: Fix q and any T subset of {1,...,q}. Use q columns, threshold k=3, and m=sum_{r=1}^q r+q-1 rows partitioned into slots of heights 1,...,q, with one separator row between slots. Initialize every entry to -H, where H=4q+4. For each r in T, put a gadget in the first r columns of slot r: for r=1 replace its cell by 4; for r>=2 replace the r by r rectangle by zeros and put 1 at each of its four corners. Its r-square has sum 4>k. Any smaller square wholly inside that gadget contains at most one corner, hence has sum at most 1. A square not wholly inside one selected gadget contains a -H entry; the entire matrix has at most 4q positive mass, so its sum is at most 4q-H=-4. Therefore side h is infeasible exactly when h is in T. The dimensions and H are independent of T, and every entry has O(log q) bits.

results.claim: Every deterministic algorithm that accesses an instance only through adaptive side-feasibility queries requires q queries in the worst case.
results.proof_sketch: By the preceding construction, every q-bit vector of positive-length feasibility answers occurs, with common dimensions and threshold. Answer 'infeasible' to each query. If an algorithm stops with some side r unqueried, both the all-infeasible vector, whose optimum is 0, and the vector in which only r is feasible, whose optimum is r, are consistent with its transcript. Hence it cannot be correct on both and must query every side on the all-infeasible transcript. This is a lower bound only in the feasibility-oracle model; it does not apply to algorithms that inspect and combine matrix entries directly.

results.claim: The feasibility-oracle obstruction persists under randomization: bounded-error randomized algorithms require Omega(q) queries in the worst case.
results.proof_sketch: Use Yao's principle. Give probability 1/2 to the all-infeasible vector and 1/(2q) to each vector having exactly one feasible side r; the arbitrary-pattern construction realizes every member with common dimensions and threshold. Fix a deterministic algorithm making at most t queries. On its all-infeasible transcript it queries at most t distinct sides. Grant it success whenever a singleton lies among them. If its output on the remaining common transcript is 0, its distributional success is at most 1/2+t/(2q). If it outputs a positive side, it loses the all-infeasible atom and can guess at most one unqueried singleton, for success at most (t+1)/(2q), which is no larger. For t<q/3 the success probability is below 2/3. Therefore any randomized algorithm correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input has worst-case query complexity Omega(q). This remains only a Boolean feasibility-oracle lower bound, not a word-RAM lower bound.

results.claim: Feasibility can alternate at every side length, and the natural no-revisit greedy extension is incorrect.
results.proof_sketch: For any n, take an n by n matrix whose first row is 1,-1,1,-1,... and whose other rows are zero, with k=0. For even l, every length-l interval of the first row sums to zero, so every l-square has sum zero. For odd l, intervals in that row sum to either 1 or -1, squares below it sum to zero, and the interval beginning in the first column sums to one. Hence F_l=0 for even l and F_l=1 for odd l, so feasibility alternates at every consecutive length. Separately, with k=1 and matrix [[2,1,1],[-3,1,1]], the side-2 sums scanned left to right are 1 and 4. A no-revisit scan accepts the first, decreases to side 1 only at the second, and can miss the earlier entry 2. It may return 1, although F_2=4 and F_1=2, so the correct answer is 0.

results.claim: The O(mn) endpoint is achievable for two nontrivial signed separable classes: multiplicative rank one and additive separability.
results.proof_sketch: Suppose first that A_ij=u_i v_j. For each l, let X_l be all length-l window sums of u and Y_l those of v. Every l-square sum is xy with x in X_l and y in Y_l. Its maximum is attained among the four products formed from min X_l, max X_l, min Y_l, and max Y_l. One-dimensional prefix sums compute these extrema in O(m+n) time per l. Over q lengths this is O(q(m+n))<=2mn. Rank one can be recognized in O(mn): choose a nonzero pivot p=A_rc and check p A_ij=A_ic A_rj everywhere; the all-zero case is immediate. Using the pivot representation, evaluate each of the four corner products divided exactly by p and then take their maximum, which also handles p<0. If A_ij=u_i+v_j, an l-square sum is l(X+Y), so F_l=l(max X_l+max Y_l), with the same time bound. Additive separability is recognized by checking A_ij=A_i1+A_1j-A_11.

results.claim: A thresholded max-plus-convolution scan embeds exactly into matrices supported on one row.
results.proof_sketch: Given integer vectors x,y of length N, define c_t=max_{i+j=t}(x_i+y_j). Put W=max(1,max|x_i|,max|y_j|), C=2W+1, H=C+W+1, and B=4N. Define a prefix sequence p_0,...,p_B as follows: p_s=H for 0<=s<=2N-2, p_s=-H for 2N+2<=s<=B, and set the three intervening values arbitrarily. Overwrite p_i=-x_i and p_{B-j}=y_j+C. Form a B by B matrix whose first row is p_{s+1}-p_s and whose other rows are zero. For l=B-t, 0<=t<=2N-2, a first-row window starting at s telescopes to p_{s+B-t}-p_s. Setting i=s and j=t-s gives C+x_i+y_j for valid convolution indices. If i or j is invalid, the corresponding H or -H value makes the window negative; every valid value is at least one. Squares below the first row sum to zero. Thus F_{B-t}=C+c_t exactly. At threshold C+K, the largest feasible encoded length corresponds to the least t with c_t<=K.

results.claim: If integer bit lengths are unbounded and bit operations are charged, an O(mn) bound independent of bit length is impossible.
results.proof_sketch: For a 1 by 1 matrix, the answer is determined by comparing its entry a with k. In an explicit-binary bit-cost model, fix a=k=2^(B-1). For every lower position r, replacing a by 2^(B-1)+2^r changes the correct answer while changing only that bit. Correctness on the equality input therefore requires ruling out all B-1 alternatives, giving Omega(B) worst-case bit cost. Hence no uniform O(mn)=O(1) bit-time bound exists even in this base case. This is only the generic input-length obstruction: it does not rule out O(mn) arithmetic/word operations and therefore does not settle the substantive bounded-word endpoint.

final_writeup:
Let q=min(m,n) and F_l be the maximum sum of an l by l square. I did not obtain either a general O(mn) word-RAM algorithm or a standard-assumption lower bound excluding one, so the requested endpoint remains unresolved.

The structural reformulation is exact. If P is the two-dimensional prefix array, an l-square sum with prefix-corner (i,j) is the mixed difference P_{i+l,j+l}-P_{i+l,j}-P_{i,j+l}+P_{i,j}. Thus the target asks for the largest offset l for which every contiguous equal-offset mixed difference is at most k: a relaxed square-Monge condition. Prefix construction and mixed differencing are inverse O(mn) transforms, so algorithms transfer both ways. This viewpoint is complexity-neutral; it does not turn the nonlocal offset conditions into local ones.

The strongest general positive result remains a linear verifier. A proposed optimum L is correct exactly when every L-square has sum at most k and, for each l>L, one supplied l-square has sum greater than k. Two-dimensional prefix sums verify this in O(mn) arithmetic/word operations. Descending exhaustive search consequently gives an exact O(mnq) worst-case algorithm, with the sharper inherited output-sensitive bound when L is close to q.

The obstruction is structural. For every subset T of {1,...,q}, there is a signed matrix with fixed threshold 3 and O(log q)-bit entries whose infeasible side lengths are exactly T. Vertically separated gadgets of total sum 4 realize selected lengths; a negative background dominates every square crossing a gadget boundary. Consequently the relaxed mixed-difference conditions across offsets can encode an arbitrary Boolean vector. A deterministic method accessing the instance only through fixed-length feasibility queries needs all q queries. The reduction also yields an Omega(q) bound for bounded-error randomized oracle algorithms: under a half all-infeasible, half uniformly singleton-feasible distribution, t queries have success at most 1/2+t/(2q), so 2/3 success needs t>=q/3. These are black-box limitations, not lower bounds on algorithms that inspect entries directly. The alternating family and 2 by 3 example separately refute monotone and no-revisit scans.

Two signed special classes attain O(mn): multiplicative rank one and additive separability. Their square sums reduce to extrema of one-dimensional window sums over all lengths. The one-row construction embeds thresholded max-plus-convolution coefficients exactly, but its dense matrix has quadratic size in the vector length and supplies no endpoint lower bound. If arbitrary integer bit lengths are charged explicitly, even a 1 by 1 comparison forces Omega(B) bit work; that input-length obstruction does not exclude O(mn) bounded-word or unit-cost time. Thus the full algorithmic question remains only partially resolved.
